A course of FSTD training and/or flight training in two phases as follows:
Phase one (EFVS 200 operations with aircraft and all equipment serviceable) —
understand the operation of equipment required for EFVS 200 operations;
understand operating limitations of the installed EFVS;
practise the use of HUD or equivalent display systems;
practise the set-up and adjustment of EFVS equipment in different conditions (e.g.
practise the monitoring of automatic flight control systems, EFVS information and
practise the interpretation of EFVS imagery;
become familiar with the features needed on the EFVS image to continue approach
(viii) practise the identification of visual references using natural vision while using EFVS
master the manual aircraft handling relevant to EFVS 200 operations including,
where appropriate, the use of the flare cue and guidance for landing;
practise coordination with other crew members; and
become proficient at procedures for EFVS 200 operations.
Phase one of the training should include the following exercises:
the required checks for satisfactory functioning of equipment, both on the ground
the use of HUD or equivalent display systems during all phases of flight;
at least one life-raft with a rated capacity of not less than the maximum number of
persons on board, stowed so as to facilitate their ready use in emergency;
at least one survival ELT (ELT(S)) for each required life-raft; and
life-saving equipment, including means of sustaining life, as appropriate to the flight to
AMC1 SPO.IDE.H.199 Life-rafts, survival ELTs and survival equipment

LIFE–RAFTS AND EQUIPMENT FOR MAKING DISTRESS SIGNALS
Each required life-raft should conform to the following specifications:
be of an approved design and stowed so as to facilitate their ready use in an emergency;
be radar conspicuous to standard airborne radar equipment;
when carrying more than one life-raft on board, at least 50 % of the rafts should be able
to be deployed by the crew while seated at their normal station, where necessary by
life-rafts that are not deployable by remote control or by the crew should be of such
weight as to permit handling by one person. 40 kg should be considered a maximum
Each required life-raft should contain at least the following:
one canopy (for use as a sail, sunshade or rain catcher) or other mean to protect
one 20 m retaining line designed to hold the life-raft near the helicopter but to release it
if the helicopter becomes totally submerged;
one survival kit, appropriately equipped for the route to be flown, which should contain
JAA TEMPORARY GUIDANCE MATERIAL, LEAFLET NO. 2 (TGL 2)
FAA AC 20-130A for en route operations;
FAA AC 20-138 for en route operations; and
If a statement of compliance with any of the following specifications or standards is found
in the acceptable documentation as listed above, the aircraft is eligible for RNAV 1/RNAV
FAA AC 20-138 for the appropriate navigation specification;
JAA TEMPORARY GUIDANCE MATERIAL, LEAFLET NO. 10 Rev1 (TGL 10);
However, if position determination is exclusively computed based on VOR-DME, the
aircraft is not eligible for RNAV 1/RNAV 2 operations.
If a statement of compliance with any of the following specifications or standards is found
in the acceptable documentation as listed above, the aircraft is eligible for RNP 1/RNP 2
FAA AC 20-138 for the appropriate navigation specification; and
Alternatively, if a statement of compliance with any of the following specifications or
standards is found in the acceptable documentation as listed above and position

continental operations. However, in these cases, loss of GNSS implies loss of RNP 1/RNP
